Paul defends the source of a message whose reception is now disputed

Verse 11 says Paul’s good news is not of human origin. Verse 12 denies two human routes: he neither received it nor was taught it. It came through revelation of Jesus Christ. The rest of the chapter gives evidence from his movements. He did not consult anyone or go to Jerusalem (verses 16–17). His first visit came three years later and lasted fifteen days (verse 18). Verse 20 swears before God that this is no lie.
Shared recognition fails when fear divides the meal

Verse 12 gives the facts: Peter ate with Gentiles and then withdrew in fear. Verse 13 says the other Jewish believers and Barnabas followed him. Verse 14 names the fault: not walking by the truth of the good news. Paul answers “before them all.” His question points to the gap. Peter himself had lived like a Gentile. Now his withdrawal pressed Gentiles to live like Jews.
Promise and shared inheritance answer the demand for another membership sign

The dispute is who counts as Abraham’s offspring and heir. Verse 16 says the promised offspring is Christ. Verse 17 says the later law cannot cancel that promise. Verses 26–28 say all who are baptized into Christ are one in him. Verse 29 draws the conclusion in two steps. If they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring. If offspring, they are heirs by promise.
Paul turns a family account into an argument about the disputed promise

Verse 21 addresses those who want to be under the law. Paul answers them from the law’s own account of Abraham (verse 22). Verse 24 says plainly that he reads it as an allegory. The two women stand for two covenants, and Hagar stands for Sinai. Verse 26 sets the free Jerusalem above against her. This is Paul’s comparison for this dispute, not a verdict on a people. Verse 31 gives its point: believers are children of the free woman.
Freedom becomes service through love rather than permission to consume others

Verse 1 said Christ set them free and warned against a yoke of bondage. Verse 13 guards that freedom from the other side. Freedom must not become an opening for the flesh. The verse then tells free people to be servants to one another. Love is the means. Verse 14 gives the reason: the whole law is fulfilled in loving a neighbor. Verse 15 shows the alternative: biting and devouring until they consume each other.
Shared burdens stand beside personal examination and patient work

Verse 1 gives a case: someone is caught in a fault. Those who restore him must be gentle and watch themselves. Verse 2 widens the case to a rule: bear one another’s burdens. It calls this fulfilling “the law of Christ.” The letter has argued against the law as a requirement for Gentiles. Here Paul names a law they do keep, and 5:14 called it love. Verse 5 adds that each still carries his own load.
